claims.text: High configurational entropy kinetically hinders atomic diffusion in equiatomic high-entropy nanoparticles.
Hindered atomic diffusion suppresses phase segregation and maintains a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution.
Maintaining the homogeneous solid solution preserves catalytic and thermoelectric performance across 473–1923 K.
The intended initial material consists of nanoparticles containing at least five metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and crystallized as a uniform single-phase solid solution.
The initial solid solution has atomic-scale elemental homogeneity.
Controlled atmospheres and uniform thermal ramping ensure that observed changes arise from intrinsic thermal effects.
An atomic-scale homogeneous random-alloy structure reflects maintained configurational entropy.
High configurational entropy increases the activation-energy barrier for atomic diffusion.
The resulting kinetic stabilization suppresses chemical demixing under high-temperature conditions.
After exposure from 473 K to 1923 K, the high-entropy nanoparticles will retain a single-phase solid solution with minimal elemental segregation.
After thermal exposure, catalytic and thermoelectric performance will remain similar to the initial baseline.
A control sample with reduced configurational entropy will undergo more phase separation than the high-entropy nanoparticles.
A control sample with reduced configurational entropy will exhibit a greater performance decline than the high-entropy nanoparticles.
Strong oxidants, thermal gradients, or redox reactions can independently drive structural or chemical changes.
Omitting one element from the nanoparticle composition reduces configurational entropy.
Kinetic stabilization may fail near the upper end of the 473–1923 K range.
